name: Branchless destination selection by pointer-array indexing
listed_description: Replace an if/else that picks which accumulator to update with an index into an array of two accumulator pointers, so the loop has no data-dependent branch.
claim_text: Branchless version of the code is 3.5 times faster than the loop with an unpredictable branch.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark loop over random 0/1 condition array accumulating into one of two sums, branchy vs array-indexed. Clang-11 on x86 mentioned for the chapter; exact CPU and flags not stated in text, numbers only in a figure image. Code in the Chapter03 directory of the companion repo.
guessed_baseline: plain if/else loop with unpredictable branch
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 3, Branchless computing, Branchless selection

name: Branchless two-expression evaluation (compute both, select by index)
listed_description: Compute both arms of a conditional unconditionally into a small array and pick the result and destination by the condition value, trading extra arithmetic for no pipeline flushes.
claim_text: The book calls the branchless transformation effective for a random condition, but a well-predicted branch beats it; only chart values are given.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, random condition array, one arm subtracts and the other multiplies two input arrays; branchy loop vs two branchless variants, repeated with a predictable condition. Numbers only in figure images (Figures 3.31 to 3.33); CPU not stated in text.
guessed_baseline: plain if/else loop with unpredictable branch
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 3, Branchless computing, Branchless computing examples

name: Bitwise or arithmetic operators in place of short-circuit && and ||
listed_description: Rewrite a compound condition that is almost always true using bitwise or addition operators so the CPU sees one branch, not several poorly predicted ones.
claim_text: Replacing logical || with addition or bitwise | gives the performance of a perfectly predicted branch; side effects are then always evaluated.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of a loop whose condition is always true but via two alternating sub-conditions, compared with a random branch, a temp-variable variant, a pre-evaluated temp vector and the arithmetic and bitwise variants. Figure 3.29, no numbers in text; Clang-11 x86 for chapter.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 3, Optimization of complex conditions

name: Pre-evaluated condition array to isolate branch misprediction
listed_description: Compute a complex boolean condition for all elements into a temporary array in a first loop, then branch on the stored values in a second loop that runs many times.
claim_text: A temporary vector of conditions gives the expected performance of a perfectly predicted branch, because every stored element is true.
book_benchmark: Same benchmark as the short-circuit entry (BM_false_branch_vtemp variant in Figure 3.29). Works only if the second loop runs much more often than the initialisation loop. No numbers in text.
guessed_baseline: inline compound condition inside the loop
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 3, Optimization of complex conditions

name: Contiguous std::vector instead of std::list for sequential traversal
listed_description: Store 1M 64-bit integers in an array or vector so traversal is sequential and prefetched, instead of in separately allocated std::list nodes.
claim_text: List access is just over 5 nanoseconds per value, almost an order of magnitude slower than about 0.6 nanoseconds per value for an array.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark write of 1M unsigned long elements to std::vector vs std::list (Figure 4.10); 8 MB vs 24 MB footprint. CPU unnamed; caches 32 KB L1, 256 KB L2, 8 MB L3 mentioned. Code in Chapter04 of the companion repo.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 4, Optimizing memory performance, Memory-efficient data structures

name: Block-allocated array (deque-style growable array)
listed_description: Allocate storage in cache-sized fixed blocks (2 KB to 16 KB) linked in a list so the container grows without copying while keeping mostly sequential access.
claim_text: Can perform almost identically to the array or vector; std::deque in most STLs is somewhat slower than vector for sequential access.
book_benchmark: No benchmark; description only, with a remark that typical std::deque implementations are slower than vector for sequential access.
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 4, Optimizing memory performance, Memory-efficient data structures

name: Sequential record rewriting into a fresh buffer instead of list of strings
listed_description: Apply change sets to string records by streaming all records into a new contiguous or block-allocated buffer, copying unchanged ones, instead of editing nodes of a std::list<std::string> in place.
claim_text: For 128-byte strings with 99% edited, sequential algorithm is approximately four times faster than random; at 1% edited it is almost a tie.
book_benchmark: Regex-driven edit of medium-length (128 byte) string records, sequential copy vs std::list<std::string> in-place replacement; at 50% edited the sequential version is about 12% faster. CPU and compiler not stated for this test.
guessed_baseline: std::list<std::string> with per-record insert and erase
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 4, Optimizing algorithms for memory performance

name: 256-bit SIMD word copy and read (AVX __m256i) versus 64-bit words
listed_description: Moving memory with SSE or AVX wide types gives more bytes per access because random read speed in words per second does not depend on word size.
claim_text: Copying 256-bit words does the job four times faster than using 64-bit words; memcpy is already optimized.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of read/write/copy of unsigned long, __m128i and __m256i over ranges from 1 KB to 1 GB (Figures 4.3 to 4.6). Book author's workstation, CPU not named, L1 32 KB, L2 256 KB, L3 8 MB.
guessed_baseline: 64-bit word copy loop (std::memcpy named as the library alternative)
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 4, The speed of memory: the numbers, The speed of random memory access

name: Signed int loop index in substring comparison
listed_description: Using int rather than unsigned int for the index in a character-by-character substring compare, in the book's std::sort substring sort example, makes the compiled loop faster.
claim_text: Unsigned bounded version 98 ms, unsigned without bound check 210 ms, signed int version 74 ms for the same sort.
book_benchmark: std::sort of 2^14 substring pointers over a 2^18-character mostly-constant string using a custom compare function in a separate file; also a Google Benchmark of the compare functions. Timed with chrono; compiler 'production compiler' unnamed in this chapter, CPU unnamed.
guessed_baseline: same compare function with unsigned int index and length bound
found_in: book: The Art of Writing Efficient Programs (2021), ch. 2, Performance measurements by example; Micro-benchmarks are lies
